section_title: How does Jesus explain the bread that gives lasting life?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 32 Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. 33 For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” 34 “Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.” 35 Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst. 36 But as I stated, you have seen Me and still you do not believe. 37 Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away. 38 For I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me. 39 And this is the will of Him who sent Me, that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day. 40 For it is My Father’s will that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.”

41 At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” 42 They were asking, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, ‘I have come down from heaven’ ?” 43 “Stop grumbling among yourselves,” Jesus replied. 44 “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day. 45 It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me— 46 not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father. 47 Truly, truly, I tell you, he who believes has eternal life. 48 I am the bread of life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. 50 This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. 51 I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”

52 At this, the Jews began to argue among themselves, “How can this man give us His flesh to eat?” 53 So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you. 54 Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. 55 For My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink. 56 Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him. 57 Just as the living Father sent Me and I live because of the Father, so also the one who feeds on Me will live because of Me. 58 This is the bread that came down from heaven. Unlike your fathers, who ate the manna and died, the one who eats this bread will live forever.”

context_lines: This extended passage belongs to the conversation after the feeding. Jesus points beyond the manna associated with Moses to the Father’s true bread, identifies Himself as that bread, and promises life and resurrection to those who come in faith.

He answers objections to His heavenly origin by speaking of the Father’s drawing and teaching. He then names His flesh as the gift for the world’s life and develops the language of receiving His flesh and blood and remaining in Him.
The connected sequence helps keep the Father’s initiative, faith, Jesus’ self-giving and His promise of resurrection together. The next section records how His hearers respond to the teaching.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian traditions agree that Jesus is the bread giving life and that people need God’s grace to come to Him. They differ over the Father’s drawing, continuing faith and how the eating language relates to Communion.

Reformed teaching describes God bringing those He has chosen willingly to Christ and preserving them to the end. Wesley reads the Father’s drawing as grace that can be resisted and the promises as calling for continuing faith. Catholic teaching also begins with God’s undeserved initiative while affirming a free response and the possibility of losing faith. ([Westminster Confession 10, 17](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [Wesley on John 6:37–44](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/); [Catechism §§1996–2002](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_one/chapter_three/article_2/ii_grace.index.html); [Catechism §162](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/iii_the_characteristics_of_faith.index.html))

The Catholic Church reads the discourse as an announcement of the Eucharist and teaches that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, with the whole Christ truly present. ([Catechism §1336](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_one/article_3/iii_the_eucharist_in_the_economy_of_salvation.html); [Catechism §§1374–1376](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_one/article_3/v_the_sacramental_sacrifice_thanksgiving_memorial_presence.html))

The Lutheran Formula of Concord explains John 6 as receiving Christ through faith, which happens through hearing the gospel and also in Communion. Lutheran teaching separately affirms that Christ’s true body and blood are received in and under the bread and wine. ([Formula of Concord VII.61–65](https://bookofconcord.org/solid-declaration/the-holy-supper/); [Large Catechism, Altar §§8–14](https://bookofconcord.cph.org/en/large-catechism/part_5/))

Calvin reads John 6 as receiving Christ continually through faith, rather than as referring directly to the Communion rite. The Westminster and Baptist confessions nevertheless teach that believers truly receive spiritual nourishment from Christ in the meal; their account is more than simply recalling a distant event. ([Calvin on John 6:53](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/6.htm); [Westminster Confession 29.5–7](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [Baptist Confession 30.1, 7](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-30))

Wesley connects the words directly with Christ’s suffering and receiving Him through faith, and only remotely, if at all, with the Lord’s Supper. This is his interpretation of the passage, rather than a denial that Christians should share the meal. ([Wesley on John 6:51–53](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/))
god_plan_lines: Deuteronomy says that manna taught dependence on God’s word, and Jesus draws on that lesson in His wilderness temptation. The bread theme belongs within that larger call to live by what God gives and says. ([Deuteronomy 8:2–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/8.htm); [Matthew 4:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/4.htm))

Hebrews connects Christ’s self-offering with redemption and a cleansed conscience for serving God. Paul connects the shared bread and cup with a people joined to Christ and one another, proclaiming His death until He returns. These passages place the gift of life within His sacrifice and the community formed through it. ([Hebrews 9:11–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/9.htm); [1 Corinthians 10:16–17](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/10.htm); [1 Corinthians 11:23–26](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/11.htm))
The promised resurrection also belongs within the victory begun by Christ’s own resurrection and ending in death’s defeat. ([1 Corinthians 15:20–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm))
current_position_lines: Our study Prayer and Faith reads Jesus as the living bread to whom the manna pointed. The manna sustained life for a time; Christ Himself gives lasting life. The study connects receiving that life with faith and continued dependence on Him. Our study also identifies the Father’s stated will here as life and resurrection for those who believe in the Son.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Prayer and Faith: Section4 The Missing Link — Christ as the Living Bread; direct developed John6:32–58/48–51/58 discussion. Narrow Christ-as-life/bread/faith/dependence conclusion, not a new ruling on drawing, perseverance or Eucharistic presence. Prayer and Faith Section1 What His Will Actually Means directly develops John6:39–40 as revealed will.
